@@52177551 <p> In April 2013 in Bangladesh , the Savar building collapsed , killing an estimated 1,300 garment workers and injuring another 2,500 in what became known as the Rana Plaza collapse . <p> The story intrigued me as an academic and global citizen wanting to find answers . <p> There is a long history of industrial accidents in Bangladesh factories , and there continue to be issues in the aftermath of these accidents . <p> This is despite decades of activism , including universities such as my own vowing to take responsibility for their supply chains . After Rana Plaza , North American and European clothing retailers , from Benetton to Joe Fresh , all claimed that this time was different . <p> They created two ambitious systems of auditing and supply-chain tracing , along with worker complaint lines , to reassure customers that their clothes were made safely and that major companies were taking responsibility . <p> In the aftermath of the accident , I worked with Maureen Benson-Rea , a business professor at the University of Auckland , to examine this supposedly game-changing set of agreements . The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ were not promising . <p> Among other things , we found an almost total lack of local labour enforcement by the Bangladeshi government , and an almost complete lack of follow-through on failed audits of multinational corporations ( in this case , clothing brands ) , including remedial actions . Seven years later , nothing has really changed for Bangladeshi workers . <p> Trendy business model <p> Corporate social responsibility , or CSR , is a burgeoning business model . Spurred by a series of scandals , it has become a mainstay of our business schools . <p> However , CSR efforts have n't stopped the continual parade of scandals , from Boeing 's 737 Max failures to the BP Deepwater Horizon oil spill and the well-known gaming of financial markets by investment houses , as depicted in books and films that include The Wolf of Wall Street and The Big Short . <p> Instead of progress towards decency in labour and environmental standards , we find ourselves in a continuing maelstrom of corporate social irresponsibility . <p> When matched with growing inequality , it 's no wonder we 're @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a reflexive reaction against big corporations . Far from being responsible citizens , large corporations are increasingly dodging paying even basic taxes . <p> There are three obvious sources of failure in CSR . <p> First source of failure : Neoliberalism <p> The first is the general move towards neoliberalism , or the faith in markets to create self-regulation by allowing companies and investment houses to make their own bets and supposedly suffer the consequences . Anyone with common sense knows that companies are wired towards profit and , in the absence of public policy , will put it above all else . <p> We should n't forget that western labour and environmental standards were the result of government policy , not markets . In fact , the minute markets fail , companies consistently cry for government bailouts , as we saw in the 1980s- ' 90s savings-and-loan crisis in the U.S. , the 2008 financial crisis and the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic -- all while financial services lobbyists block reforms to prevent future crises . <p> This has been enabled more generally because companies have been able to influence regulation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cases push false counter-narratives , such as climate change denial . In the Global South , where governments lack rule of law and institutional capacity , companies have a long history of feeding corruption and influencing governments to cut " sweetheart deals " to benefit them financially . CSR is important for marketing , not for the bottom line . <p> Second source of failure : Globalized production <p> The second source of failure is related to the globalization of production . Governments in the Global South have consistently voiced their opposition to rigorous labour or environmental standards on the grounds that companies will simply move their factories elsewhere . <p> The fight for jobs , consistent investment and the desperate need for access to multinational corporation 's retail outlets explains why coffee farmers , for example , take pennies on the dollar compared to large coffee retail chains like Starbucks . <p> Simply put , governments and workers in the Global South have limited bargaining leverage when it comes to large transnationals , and workers and local communities have even less . Clearly , a global system is needed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ point to the plethora of global initiatives , from the Global Reporting Indicators to the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative , coming in the wake of The Global Compact , an agreement championed by the United Nations . These initiatives were ostensibly aimed at setting guidelines and demonstrating responsible behaviour . <p> Companies are spending an estimated US$20 billion per year on CSR to comply with these standards , and pay an army of consultants and NGO auditors to verify such . As I argue in a recent article in Global Affairs and in a special edition of the Journal of Developing Societies , such efforts are vacuous and more effective at public relations than at changing real-life outcomes . <p> Third source of failure : No transparency <p> In fact , there is a continuing lack of transparency in CSR initiatives -- most of them largely dependent on businesses self-reporting their efforts -- that socially responsible investment indices rely upon . Audits are specious and full of conflicts of interest because companies actually employ auditors to verify their compliance . Most of the investment indicators do not even dispatch personnel @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Governments that receive millions in royalties from multinational corporations for the right to mine , for instance , do not report what they do with the revenues , and so corruption is apparent . In short , there is no real accountability or enforcement of CSR standards . <p> The bottom line is that companies are in no way taking responsibility for changing anything concretely . Their CSR reports delve into taxes paid , one-off projects and related expenditures , not on changes in real-life outcomes . <p> In assessing mining sites over the past four years , I have seen communities without basic services -- no running water , electricity or roads -- located next to international mines that have been rewarded or lauded for their CSR initiatives . <p> A government approved by a global transparency body even censored my survey of community sentiments about mining , and questions about the use of revenues , though it could not deny the veracity of my findings . When I asked the global transparency body to intervene , they said that there was nothing they could do . <p> It @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ plagued by continual conflict . Until there are global standards for outcomes , transparency through the supply and revenue chains , conflict-free auditing , enforced labour rights and environmental standards , we will continue to see local impoverishment , hazardous waste and tragic labour accidents as resources in the Global South are exploited by companies in the West . <p> Make our voices heard <p> A handful of well-meaning activists ca n't make any real difference in this fight . <p> Consumers can make their voices heard by pushing politicians to leverage access to western markets to set up a global system that matters , with standards that can be verified . <p> Just as we do n't allow our companies to sell products that use child labour , pollute the environment or bypass communities where resources are exploited in our own countries , we can simply apply the same principles for products made anywhere . <p> Extending this basic principle -- already the standard for domestic products -- would immediately force companies and host governments to change their practices , creating a level playing field for organizations that want @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ routine . <p> Such a policy shift would change the world overnight , raising the living standards for millions and saving capitalism from itself . <p> We welcome your feedback and encourage you to share your thoughts . @@52178055 <h> Purchase of St. Luke 's Marsh ' biggest acquisition ' by Ducks Unlimited in Ontario <p> After years of trying , Ducks Unlimited Canada has purchased the 488-acre St. Luke 's Marsh in Dover Township , which is one of the few remaining coastal wetlands on Lake St. Clair in Southwestern Ontario . Contributed photojpg , CD <p> After years of trying , Ducks Unlimited Canada has finally bought the almost 200-hectare ( 488-acre ) St. Luke 's Marsh , one of the few remaining coastal wetlands on Lake St. Clair in Southwestern Ontario . <p> " It 's huge , " manager of land securement Erling Armson said of the organization purchasing the land in Dover Township , near Pain Court . " In terms of cost , this has been the biggest acquisition we 've ever done in Ontario . It was a few million dollars . " <p> Armson said the next step will be developing a management plan for the provincially significant area , which also includes other mixed wildlife habitats . <p> " We 'll be taking into account all kinds of things , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ will be protecting and making sure the wetland remains intact and is valuable for waterfowl and other wildlife and species at risk . " <p> Ducks Unlimited will also be looking at " what kind of people uses may be permitted there in the future , " Armson said . <p> He added this could include bird watching , public access and potential hunting . <p> St. Luke 's Marsh is located beside the publicly owned 357-hectare ( 882-acre ) St. Clair National Wildlife Area , which shelters more than 60 species of birds and 35 federally listed species at risk , such as king rail , least bittern and eastern fox snake . <p> Given the proximity of the two properties , Armson said Ducks Unlimited would be " open to a lot of options , " including an access link between the two wetland areas . <p> The development of the marsh 's management plan will involve speaking with interested parties , including the Canadian Wildlife Service , which manages the wildlife area , he said . <p> Armson said Ducks Unlimited had wanted to buy this wetland @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ group of Americans with the St. Luke 's Club -- for years . <p> When Ducks Unlimited first approached the previous U.S. owners a number of years ago about buying the land , the deal would have included selling it through a U.S. corporation , Armson said . <p> The property was then listed for US$3.5 million . <p> However , Armson said the most recent owner , an Ontario resident , agreed to sell the property in Canadian dollars , not requiring Ducks Unlimited to purchase a U.S. corporation in the deal . <p> He said there were some U.S. buyers interested in the property but , then COVID-19 hit . <p> Since the pandemic closed the Canada-U.S. border , the interested American buyers were unable to visit to view the property . <p> Chatham native Paul Brisco , who specializes in hunting properties through his London-based company Corland Realty Inc. , brokered the sale . <p> " I 've sold a number of hunting club properties and they are expensive properties , absolutely , " Brisco said . " What 's unique , this time , is the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ which I still have for sale , and allowing Ducks Unlimited to just preserve the marsh separately . " <p> A longtime Ducks Unlimited supporter , Brisco , a life sponsor and past board member , said he was " very pleased and proud to see Ducks Unlimited acquire ( this property ) . " <p> He added Ducks Unlimited members would like to see the conservation organization " find some way in their management plan to accommodate some hunting . " <p> But Brisco noted that decision is up to how Ducks Unlimited sees it from a management perspective . <p> The project was supported by the federal government 's Natural Heritage Conservation Program , which is part of Canada 's Nature Fund . <p> The purchase of the marsh supports the Government of Canada 's target of conserving 25 per cent of Canada 's lands by 2025 and its objectives for the recovery of wild species listed under the federal Species at Risk Act , stated a media release . <p> In congratulating Ducks Unlimited for acquiring the the marsh , federal Environment Minister Jonathan Wilkinson noted " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ habitat , and play a role in the fight against climate change . " <p> St. Luke 's Marsh is one of 22 conservation properties held by Ducks Unlimited Canada within the Great Lakes watershed , accounting for almost 2,833 hectares of protected habitat .

@@52178689 <h> Muneesh Sharma and Madi Kennedy : Time for B.C. to pick up the pace on building retrofits <p> With election day in the rearview mirror , many British Columbians are looking to the provincial government to take strong leadership on urgent economic and social priorities in concert with bold action on climate change . <p> Upgrading the buildings where we live and work ticks all of these boxes by reducing carbon pollution ; increasing safety , public health , and housing affordability ; and aiding in economic recovery by creating thousands of local jobs using mostly local materials . <h> What is PACE ? <p> PACE financing is an innovative " green " loan instrument developed in California in 2008 that overcomes the capital constraints that many buildings owners face when contemplating upgrades . The concept is simple : building owners borrow funds to complete retrofits , such as replacing gas furnaces with heat pumps , upgrading windows , adding solar panels , or even making seismic improvements . <p> What makes these loans different is they are registered on the property title , not to the owner , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are repaid in installments added to property taxes over the retrofit 's lifespan . PACE programs are now active in 37 U.S. states , resulting in almost 300,000 retrofit projects and US$16.5 billion in economic impacts . <p> PACE , which enjoys cross-sector support , is attractive to commercial and residential property owners because they can fund projects with no out-of-pocket costs . PACE 's transferability from one owner to the next with the sale of the property means that building owners are only on the hook for the cost of a retrofit during the period they are benefitting from it . <p> With flexible financing terms and repayment periods up to 30 years , it 's possible to take on deep , whole-building retrofits with substantial energy and carbon savings . The annual utility-bill savings for a PACE project sometimes surpass the yearly repayments ( levied on property-tax bills ) so that property owners can be cash-flow positive immediately . That means building owners have more money to spend on other capital projects , expenses , or business expansion . <h> Can PACE work in B.C. ? <p> We @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ growing interest via Union of B.C. Municipalities resolutions . Adopting a provincewide program would help cities meet climate goals without saddling cities with debt . <p> In September , the government committed to investing $2 million in a PACE roadmap and pilot program through its Economic Recovery Plan . This investment is welcome , but sound policies can fail through poor execution . Without scale and continuity , a pilot program would likely not achieve the desired outcome . The U.S. experience shows that it takes time and scale to create a PACE ecosystem where property owners , underwriters , appraisers , financiers , and contractors understand PACE and are comfortable with its promotion and use . <h> How can we get to implementation ? <p> PACE BC -- an alliance of city councillors , business owners , and environmental organizations -- is asking the provincial government to unlock PACE for British Columbians through enabling legislation . To help the government move quickly , we 've consulted with industry and experts and drafted legislation that would allow any municipality to opt into a provincewide PACE program . <p> The government @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . PACE financing will be a game changer for owners looking to invest in protecting the homes and buildings we live , work , and play in . Unlocking PACE early in the government 's new mandate is critical for building on the economic-recovery investments expected to flow to retrofits. 
@@52178697 <h> Let 's point Chrystia Freeland 's compass to nature <p> Finance Minister Chrystia Freeland recently used the reassuring metaphor of a government compass to guide Canadians through the uncharted waters of the pandemic to a safe harbour . <p> A compass works by detecting signals that nature sends from the Earth 's magnetic fields . Nature is indeed sending us strong signals , and , if we pay attention , the direction to a sustainable and healthy future for all Canadians is clear . <p> Globally , one million animal and plant species are threatened with extinction , many within decades , and more than ever before in human history . In Canada , which is the custodian of much of the Earth 's lands , forests , fresh water and ocean shorelines , more than half of wildlife populations are in decline . <p> What is also increasingly evident is how the destruction of nature imperils our economy and our shared future . <p> According to the recent World Economic Forum report on global risks , how humans grow and harvest food , produce energy , dispose of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ balance of clean air , water and life that we and all other species need to survive . Intact habitat can be protected , and degraded habitat restored . Investments in nature can help halt biodiversity loss , provide nature-based solutions to climate change , and generate economic opportunity , good jobs , and significant financial returns . <p> Just as families count their income and debt -- and governments calculate benchmarks for fiscal responsibility -- the powerful economic value of nature should also be counted . <p> For example , in 2017-18 alone , visitor spending at Parks Canada sites contributed $2.6 billion to Canada 's GDP and $449 million in tax revenues across multiple levels of government . Charge up those headphones ! <p> It was fortunate in some ways that the early days of the pandemic coincided with the start of gardening season . When I had to cancel a trip to visit my parents in Ontario , I drew solace from researching pollinator-friendly plants and starting tomatoes from seed . Knowing that many others were doing the same made it feel like a hopeful thing to do . However , as the pandemic dragged on and news of other crises started to make headlines -- wildfires , overdose deaths , low salmon returns -- my optimism declined . <p> But I kept going outside , staking and re-staking my tomato plants , revelling in how green they smelled , how heavy the stems became as the fruit ripened , the yellow streaks they left on my arms . <p> Now that the tomatoes are long gone and case numbers are increasing again , I wonder how I @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of my summer -- to fly or not to fly -- is behind me ; now comes the grief and regret . Should I have visited my parents while the numbers were low ? <p> I call my father . Normally when I visit , we take long walks together . The colours came early this year , he tells me ; the leaves are already gone . When I ask him to talk with me about listening , it is partly because he is a musician and this is one of his favourite topics , but it is also because I have an idea . <p> " Dad , " I say , reaching toward something I 've been feeling but ca n't quite put into words , " Do you think listening to music could be another way to garden ? " <p> Long before the pandemic began , experts were telling us that gardening is good for our health . In addition to the general benefits people experience while in nature ( decreased blood pressure and anxiety , elevated mood ) , gardening provides a means of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ pandemic , it has calmed my racing mind , reduced tension in my body and given me a sense of self-sufficiency . <p> As my father often reminds me , the beneficial effects of music are also well-known . Today I ask , how do those effects work ? Do I have to listen to a certain kind of music ? <p> " Actually , " says my father , " there are many different kinds of music that can be helpful . And the more you like what you are listening to , the more open you are to experiencing its positive effects . " <p> However -- and this part is crucial -- how you feel about a given piece of music does not entirely determine its effects on you . <p> Music is , in the first place , a pattern of vibrations in the air , and these are registered by your body , regardless of what you think of it . Your body , my father reminds me , is also composed of vibrations : the heart , breath and brain all function as pulsing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> These systems are constantly moving toward synchronization -- with one another and with external stimuli . This process , called entrainment , is one of the mechanisms through which music can have calming effects , even when you are not paying attention to it . <p> " Think of the way windshield wipers move together to clean a window without bumping into one another , " says my father . When you listen to music , your heart rate , breathing and brain waves all adjust to the vibrations that music creates . Music with a slower tempo also slows you down , and this generates feelings of calm and well-being . <p> " Well , " he says , " a room that is filled with the vibrations of music is fundamentally different than a quiet one , as far as your body is concerned . " <p> In other words , it feels different . Because you are not separate from the music , you are surrounded by it . <p> This reminds me of how my patio changed once I 'd filled it with plants . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to how it felt : the smell and texture of plants around me , the sounds of birds and rustling leaves , the warmth of the sun as I worked . These sensations made it easier to step back from anxious thought processes , immerse myself in simple tasks and become aware of my surroundings . I probably started breathing more deeply , too . Gardening became a kind of listening . <p> " Because I was n't just standing in front of my plants , looking at them , " I tell my father , " I was inside the garden , I was surrounded by it . " <p> The environmental character of both music and gardening is key to appreciating their restorative potential . When we bring music into a space , we are , like a gardener , helping to create our own environment . Even if it is an indoor environment , lacking the multisensorial qualities of a garden , this modestly creative act can restore a sense of well-being and agency . <p> At the same time , the process of finding music that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and discover new forms of resilience . Experts can give you a place to start , but there are many different ways to listen to music . The important part is to pay attention to how different sonic environments make you feel . It is not just the ears that listen , says my father , but also the heart . <p> After I hang up , I reflect on something that I have never understood before about the way my father thinks of music . On the one hand , he says , it supports you , helps you relax . On the other , it changes you . For me , these two things do not usually go together . <p> But then I remember another thing my father often says -- that our emotional and intellectual responses to music are conditioned by a lifetime of experiences -- and the pieces fall into place . To benefit fully from the effects of music on your body , you have to get beyond that conditioning and open yourself to feeling something different ( which is much easier to do @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ up in the 1950s . Music was his passion , but he felt pressure to be responsible and get a real job , so he became a high school teacher . For most of my childhood , music was for evenings and weekends . I was a teenager when he finally shifted to part-time teaching so he could devote himself to music more seriously . I guess he knows a lot about conditioning , and the power of moving beyond it . <p> Of course change is often painful , especially if it is forced on us . But it can help us to see things about ourselves that are normally hidden . The combination @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ there is more contact between humans and stressed animal populations , which makes the transmission of novel viruses increasingly likely . It seems we may be entering an era of accelerating , widely-distributed risk . <p> In this context , the act of listening to music may seem pathetically out of step with the scale and scope of the crisis . And perhaps it is ; perhaps an increase in humility is in part what the pandemic calls us to cultivate . <p> But it is also true that listening to music , the way it speaks to some of the more vulnerable parts of ourselves , is essential to our ability to respond to what is happening around us . <p> Another way of coping with chronic stress is to seek pleasurable opportunities for escape -- through , for example , television , movies , social media . @@52180395 <p> Climate change , which describes long-term changes to temperature and typical weather , is accelerating at an alarming pace -- and the impacts are hard to ignore . Let 's take a look at some changes to our ocean . <h> 3 Ways Climate Change Affects Our Ocean <h> Rising sea levels <p> Sea levels are rising at the fastest rate in 3,000 years . From 2018 to 2019 , the global sea level rose to 6.1 millimeters . Sure , a few millimeters does n't sound like a lot , until you hear that the average , since 1993 , has been 3.2 millimeters per year . That means that last year we doubled the global average from the past twenty years ! The same report shares that the U.S. East Coast 's average is actually three to four times the global average . The ocean is rising , and it 's rising fast . <p> The two major causes are thermal expansion ( warm water expands ) , and melting glaciers and ice sheets . Why should we care ? Rising sea levels increase the amount and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ destroy wildlife habitats on the shoreline , interfere with coastal farming , and contaminate potable water sources . <h> Ocean acidification <p> Ocean acidification is a chemical imbalance that stems from large amounts of carbon dioxide . Put simply , it increases the concentration of hydrogen ions and reduces the amount of carbonate ions . Shellfish and other sea life rely on carbonate ions to grow their shells and thrive . But with fewer carbonate ions , shells become thin and brittle , growth slows down , and death rates increase . Since the Industrial Revolution , ocean acidity has increased by 30% . With large shellfish die-offs , the whole marine food chain is affected -- not the best news for the multi-billion dollar fishing industry . <h> Extreme weather events <p> With more heat in the atmosphere and warmer ocean surface temperatures , the world is experiencing an increase in the intensity and frequency of extreme weather events . For example , research suggests that the number of Category 4 and 5 hurricanes -- characterized by higher wind speeds and more precipitation -- is steadily increasing . To @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ along coastlines will exacerbate their impact . We 're predicting that coastal engineers and planners will be busy in the coming years . <h> Mitigating These Effects With Data <p> As demonstrated above , after years of emitting greenhouse gases , the effects of climate change are very evident . It 's time to collectively mitigate and reduce our carbon footprint . <p> We 're going to come out and just say it -- we believe it starts with better data . <p> The current scale , pace , and practice of ocean scientific discovery and observation are not keeping up with the changes in ocean and human conditions . Current data is siloed and inaccessible -- hindering a unified knowledge base for strategies and policy making . <h> Here are some ways that data needs to improve : <p> Affordability : According to the Global Ocean Science Report ( compiled by UNESCO 's Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission ) ocean research is currently led by a small number of industrialized countries . Why ? Because they can afford investments in data technology . Many coastal nations are not involved in building @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ tools . Research is expensive . <p> By providing real-time information in actionable forms , this technology is incredibly useful for driving innovation . In order to accelerate the co-creation of knowledge and strategies , these tools need to be accessible to developing countries as well . Affordability and accessibility is the driving force behind Sofar Ocean 's Spotter buoys , which you can read more about here . <p> Open data sharing : A major stumbling block to universal data synthesis is ownership . Government agencies , research , and private companies are all key players in ocean data collection and management , keeping these insights locked away for their own specific purposes . <p> Data tagging , federated data networks , and data lakes should be combined to create a new era of open and automated ocean data access . Governments can lead the way by declassifying and sharing data that are relevant to ocean science and management . They can also incentivize companies and researchers to share data by making it a condition for access to public resources , such as funding for ocean research , permits @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fishing . <h> Making Waves Requires Momentum <p> A molecule of CO2 emitted in India or China has the same effect on the climate system as a molecule emitted in the United States . No matter where we are , climate change affects us all the same . <p> Transformative changes require a unified approach . And we believe that starts with data . <p> NetNewsledger.com or NNL offers news , information , opinions and positive ideas for Thunder Bay , Ontario , Northwestern Ontario and the world . A frightening thought given the sudden death toll , health implications and economic disruption caused by COVID-19 , a pandemic , caused by pathogen jumping between species as a result of environmental degradation and climate change . <p> It is predicted that the COVID-19 pandemic will be among a series @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ climate change across the world , including fires , floods , droughts , typhoons and other negative climate events , evidence of which we have already seen in the last 12 months with the wild fires in California and Australia to mention a few . <p> The challenge now globally is to build resilience and address the Paris climate targets by reducing greenhouse gas emissions . From a financing perspective it is estimated that nearly 50% of the risk exposures of Euro area institutions , are directly or indirectly linked to risks stemming from climate change1 . <p> In Europe , the European Commission launched the ' European Green Deal ' as its roadmap to build a circular , sustainable economy and this has been refocussed on in recent months in the context of COVID-19 ( the " Green Deal " ) . <p> Looking at the strategy and the string of announcements it can be hard to make sense of the various strategies , initiatives and the terminology , not to mention how the strands involved integrate overall . <h> Targets <p> In order to meet the net zero @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and the Paris Agreement , the 2030 targets involve a revised minimum 55% cut in GHG emissions2 , 40% renewable energy consumption and 41% renewable energy savings . It is estimated that an additional annual investment of ? 175 to ? 290 billion will be required to achieve these targets . <h> Background to the Green Framework and Initiatives <p> The European Commission appointed a high level expert group on sustainable finance ( HLEG ) in 2016 to produce a report and deliver recommendations to develop a roadmap for sustainable finance in Europe . Its final report , delivered in January 2018 , and adopted by the Commission , forms the basis of its ' Action Plan , Financing Sustainable Growth ' ; a lattice work of measures that seek to support the achievement of these targets , underpinned by the Green Deal . <h> The Green Deal <p> The Green Deal seeks to mobilise over ? 1 trillion in sustainable investment over the next decade to fund transition to the low carbon economy and facilitate sustainable investment by private investors and public sector by delivering funding to support the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the EU budget ; " ? 114bn national co-financing ; " ? 279bn through InvestEU ; " ? 143bn through the Just Transition Fund <p> The European Commission President , Ursula von der Leyen recently pledged to put the Green Deal at the heart of the COVID-19 stimulus response and announced the EU 's 2030 target was being increased from a 40% GHG reduction to a 55% reduction in GHG ( compared to 1990 levels ) . As part of that commitment , a further review of all existing EU climate legislation is underway to reflect this 55% emission reduction target . @@32321386 <h> Article Sidebar <h> Share this Story : Small steps , big gains : Mulch your leaves <h> Trending <p> Postmedia may earn an affiliate commission from purchases made through our links on this page . <h> Article content <p> What difference can I make ? As a homeowner it 's a reasonable question to ask when the topic of global warming comes up . <p> But the reality is that minor adjustments to the way we live ... small steps that often do n't require a lot of effort , can translate into big results when it comes to climate change . And often these steps save you money as well . <h> Small steps , big gains : Mulch your leavesBack to video <p> Take leaves for example . Think of the time you spend going out buying leaf bags , not to mention the cost of gas and wear and tear on your car to get you there and back . Over the years , it adds up . <p> Then there 's the time it takes to rake and bag those leaves and haul them out @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ -- your money , to pay for those big trucks , the fuel and drivers needed to pick up your leaves and take them to the dump . <p> Then there 's the environmental impact of those gas or diesel burning vehicles ( anyone seen an electric powered one yet ? ) driving down your street . <h> Advertisement <p> Story continues below <p> This advertisement has not loaded yet , but your article continues below . <h> Article content continued <p> Think those expenses do n't add up ? Just for downtown Toronto it costs $10 million to pick up leaves ... or $100 million every decade . Run those numbers across the country and it would n't be unreasonable to peg that cost at $1 billion during the same period . <p> So what if you make the small change of mulching your leaves and redistributing them around your home instead ? <p> As cited by the City of Toronto website , the benefits are many , including : adding much needed nutrients to your lawn and garden , helping to maintain soil moisture , controlling weeds and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ soil warmer in the winter and cooler in the summer . <p> All of this can translate into less time and money spent on fertilizer , weeding and overall lawn and garden maintenance . <p> I started mulching the leaves on our lawn where we live in Collingwood a few years ago , much to the horror of our neighbours . And since starting to do that , we 've stopped watering and fertilizing our lawn altogether . Sure our grass is far from perfect , but we are n't slaves to our lawn either , like some of our neighbours are . <p> While out for a walk a week ago , I was pleasantly surprised to discover that I 'm not alone when it comes to being a mulching convert . As I strolled by the home of neighbour and local artist Anke Lex , she was busily running her lawn mower over the fallen leaves . <p> " I 've been mulching leaves on and off for about 20 years , " Lex says . And her advice ? " You ca n't chop too many at @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ dry . " But by taking a gradual , patient approach to mulching " sometimes I do n't need to rake any leaves at all . And if I do have to rake some , I try to keep most of them on our property ( including ) composting some for our fern patch . " <h> Advertisement <p> Story continues below <p> This advertisement has not loaded yet , but your article continues below . <h> Article content continued <p> So what 's Lex 's overall takeaway , having mulched her leaves now over two decades ? " It 's much less work , " than the conventional bagging approach , " she says . <p> From my own experience , it 's also a lot more enjoyable to go for a spin on your lawn with your mower ( mine 's electric by the way so less noise and no fumes ) and marvel as you cut a swath through the leaves ... versus the back-breaking work of bagging . <p> It 's true that some cities are doing their best to take yard waste and convert it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is that if they do n't , the rotting leaves produce methane , which is the most potent greenhouse gases in the earth 's atmosphere . And there 's an added cost for them to go down that path as well . <p> To give you an idea of how cities feel about what we should do with our leaves , consider what they say on the City of Ottawa 's website . The site states : " leave your leaves ! You can use them as a natural mulch . <p> Rather than bagging leaves for curbside pick-up , put them in your gardens . This takes pressure off our waste collection crews and helps us keep serving you during the second wave of COVID-19 . Plus , your flowerbeds will thank you in the Spring . " <p> And yes , what you do on the home front ... even small steps , do add up . Consider numbers coming out of the U.S. , which is often a good indicator of what 's going on here in Canada in terms of household and city trends . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ which include leaves , created about 35.2 million tons of waste in 2017 , which is about 13% of all municipal waste generation . That 's a lot of methane gas . <p> The small step of mulching your leaves will save you money , enhance your garden and yard ... and make a positive contribution to the big picture with respect to doing your part to help reduce global warming . Small steps . Big gains . And as a homeowner , something you can feel good about . <p> Mark Wessel lives in Collingwood , Ont. and is a passionate advocate for living more sustainably at home and in the greater community . @@52181389 <h> Arctic animals adapting to climate change , but it may be causing declines : study <p> In this undated file photo , caribou from the Porcupine caribou herd migrate onto the coastal plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge in northeast Alaska . File photo by The Associated Press/U.S . Fish and Wildlife Service <p> A huge new archive of how animals move across the Arctic from season to season gives the clearest picture yet of how species from eagles to caribou are evolving in the face of climate change and hints at why some of them are in decline . <p> " This is evolution , " said Mark Hebblewhite , a University of Montana biologist who 's one of 148 co-authors of the study published Thursday in the journal Science . <p> " These are just as much evolutionary responses to climate change as environmental changes . " <p> The paper combines -- for the first time , the authors say -- millions of data points on thousands of animals from different herds , flocks and 96 species into one archive . <p> " Oftentimes , people @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <h> What people are reading <p> " They look at climate effects on one population at a time . It 's very difficult to see the forest for the trees . We 've pulled together data on dozens of populations across the entire Arctic for up to 18 years . " <p> The results confirm one thing that has been suspected for years , said Hebblewhite . As the Arctic warms , caribou cows are giving birth earlier and earlier -- up to more than two weeks sooner for some herds . <p> " ( That ) is a big effect , " he said . <p> It means something has changed in the internal wiring that governs when caribou young are born . <p> Similar changes are appearing in other animals . @@52181843 <h> Solar panel waste issues <p> Solar panels are an increasingly important source of renewable power that will play an essential role in fighting climate change . They are also complex pieces of technology that become big , bulky sheets of electronic waste at the end of their lives -- and right now , most of the world does n't have a plan for dealing with that . <p> But we 'll need to develop one soon , because the solar e-waste glut is coming . By 2050 , the International Renewable Energy Agency projects that up to 78 million metric tons of solar panels will have reached the end of their life , and that the world will be generating about 6 million metric tons of new solar e-waste annually . While the latter number is a small fraction of the total e-waste humanity produces each year , standard electronics recycling methods do n't cut it for solar panels . Recovering the most valuable materials from one , including silver and silicon , requires bespoke recycling solutions . And if we fail to develop those solutions along with policies @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ will happen . <p> " If we do n't mandate recycling , many of the modules will go to landfill , " said Arizona State University solar researcher Meng Tao , who recently authored a review paper on recycling silicon solar panels , which comprise 95 percent of the solar market . <p> Solar panels are composed of photovoltaic ( PV ) cells that convert sunlight to electricity . When these panels enter landfills , valuable resources go to waste . And because solar panels contain toxic materials like lead that can leach out as they break down , landfilling also creates new environmental hazards . <p> Most solar manufacturers claim their panels will last for about 25 years , and the world did n't start deploying solar widely until the early 2000s . As a result , a fairly small number of panels are being decommissioned today . PV Cycle , a nonprofit dedicated to solar panel take-back and recycling , collects several thousand tons of solar e-waste across the European Union each year , according to director Jan Clyncke . The bottom line is a lot of lives depend to a greater or lesser extent on how the university handles these investments . <p> At the same time , inaction should not be confused with necessary action born of careful consideration . Given UW 's strong commitment to fighting climate change -- including a vow to be carbon neutral by 2050 -- we think it 's inevitable that the university will eventually cut its ties with the fossil fuel industry . After all , UW signed the Responsible Investment Charter for universities in June , confirming its commitment to considering environmental and social factors when it invests . <p> So let the consideration begin : The first argument for divestment is moral and based on overwhelming scientific evidence . The carbon emissions that come from burning fossil fuels are the major reason the planet 's atmosphere is overheating , sea levels are rising and we 're witnessing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The only way to avoid global catastrophe , climate scientists agree , is by keeping between two-thirds and four-fifths of fossil fuels in the ground . That wo n't happen if investors keep paying to take it out . <p> The second argument for divestment is , perhaps surprisingly , economic . If Canada and the 194 other countries that signed the 2016 Paris Agreement on climate change keep their word and rapidly embrace alternative energy sources , the petroleum industry will become a shadow of its former self . <p> So if UW 's governors truly want to protect the school 's endowment and pension funds , they should realize investing in fossil fuels is becoming a risky business . Indeed , a recent study from Truzaar Dordi , a UW doctoral candidate in sustainable management , concluded the university potentially lost upwards of $20 million between 2011 and 2015 through its fossil fuel investments . <p> No one should expect a cold-turkey divestment from fossil fuels . The timing of it all would be crucial . The decision when to abandon this industry could have a huge impact @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and how much is there for its pension and endowment funds . On the plus side , perhaps divestment could spur more profitable investments in more environmentally friendly businesses . But this could take months , even years . <p> The divestment file will be back on the board of governor 's agenda when it meets next in February . The board should use the coming months to explore and weigh this important issue . And it should remember that in a ranking of more than 760 of the world 's top universities , based on the United Nations ' Sustainable Development Goals , UW is currently No. 16 . <p> It has a reputation to uphold . And part of that reputation is for being a wise and fearless leader . <h> Loading ... <h> More from The Record &amp; Partners <h> More Opinion <h> Top Stories <p> Copyright owned or licensed by Toronto Star Newspapers Limited . @@52188919 <p> Demonstrators march down a main street during an anti-racism event in Red Deer , Alta. , Sunday , Oct. 4 , 2020 . <p> Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press <p> Many Canadians have experienced intense emotions watching the election unfold in our neighbour to the south . Those of us fighting for social justice have feared the possibility of four more years of Donald Trump and the continuing destructive impact on society , well beyond the U.S. borders . We experience something visceral and deeply personal when we see the dehumanization of those who belong to communities with less power and privilege . Speaking as Chinese-Canadians , the increased anti-Asian racism this year has increased our sense of being the " other " -- being the perpetual foreigner . All our institutions , including the powerful media , must do better to ensure our social cohesion and cherish our collective humanity . <p> Chinese-Canadians continue to be treated as foreigners , despite our over 150 years of history in this nation . Nov. 7 , 2020 , marked the 135th anniversary of the Last Spike ceremony for finishing the Canadian @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ labourers were paid less than other workers and did the most dangerous jobs ; hundreds died and were often buried in unmarked graves . Our community 's contribution to this nation-building was repaid with 67 years of legislated racism , first with the exorbitant Chinese Head Tax in 1885 to restrict Chinese immigration , followed by the Chinese Exclusion Act that banned Chinese immigration outright in 1923 until 1947 . <p> Story continues below advertisement <p> Despite our long history in Canada , today Chinese-Canadians are still seen as outsiders who bring in diseases or drive up the housing market . With the rising tensions between Canada and China -- a country which is not even the birthplace of many Chinese-Canadians -- our loyalty to Canada is increasingly being questioned . <p> The pandemic has exposed how deep-seated anti-Chinese racism is in Canada . Across the country , social media has been flooded with heart-wrenching reports of verbal and physical attacks on Chinese-Canadians and other Asian-Canadians . <p> With Black Lives Matter , and other anti-racism movements across North America , more Canadians are becoming aware of the existence of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ too many Canadians either regard this as an issue that exists only south of the border , or that racism is just a matter of " a few bad apples . " <p> Sensationalism in the media gives lots of attention to explicitly racist incidents , without shining enough light on the everyday lived experiences of racialized people who face systemic barriers in the workplace , health care , justice system , and elsewhere . Nor have the media done enough of a deep dive into Canada 's history of colonization of Indigenous peoples and the transatlantic slave trade , as well as the continuing impact of such atrocities . <p> As the Far Right movement has taken to social media to spread hate and misinformation , the role of traditional media as a source of trusted information has become ever more importantThe media hold tremendous power as the disseminator of information to the general public . But with that power , media also have an obligation to ensure that they do not become part of the problem . <p> To help move our society from one where racialized folks @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ where all people belong as equal participants , influential media outlets have the power and opportunity to step up and support inclusion and belonging for all . <p> Media outlets need to become more inclusive and involve all racialized communities in issues of interests to all Canadians , and not just stories that are perceived as affecting them only . For instance , do n't interview Chinese-Canadians only when the media are doing a story on China and Hong Kong , or on the real estate market in Vancouver , but talk to us also about the Canadian economy , or climate change . We share very similar interests , experiences and expertise with all Canadians . <p> Story continues below advertisement <p> It 's important for media outlets to adopt an anti-racist approach to their work , including systemic policies and practices . They must be mindful of the impact of choices for stories , headlines and content , to avoid worsening racism or reinforcing the stereotype of Chinese-Canadians and others as perpetual foreigners . <p> Journalists and media leaders need to appreciate and understand every racialized community as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ entity . No person of colour or Indigenous person should be expected to speak for their entire community before their perspective is rendered worthy of publication . <p> The past several years of turmoil both in the United States and in Canada have taught us that our democracy is fragile , and that structural racism , if left unchecked , poses a serious risk to social cohesion . There 's so much damage to be undone when those with power and privilege try to dehumanize others . Each of us experiences racism and forms of " othering " in different and deeply personal ways . By working as a bridge , media can amplify the true reality of our entire society , and use its incredible power to transform how we see ourselves and each other . We need to start reclaiming some of our humanity and rebuilding our society based on principles of justice and equality . <p> Keep your Opinions sharp and informed . Get the Opinion newsletter . @@52189047 <h> The Government of Canada finalizes regulations to improve air quality and protect human health <p> OTTAWA , ON , Nov. 10 , 2020 /CNW/ - The Government of Canada 's number one priority remains keeping Canadians safe and supporting families and businesses through the COVID-19 pandemic . Protecting our health also means taking steps to keep our air clean . <p> New national regulations to reduce air pollution from the petroleum and petrochemical sectors will improve air quality for nearby communities and workers . ( CNW Group/Environment and Climate Change Canada ) <p> Today , the Minister of Environment and Climate Change , the Honourable Jonathan Wilkinson , announced that the Government of Canada has finalized national regulations that will reduce pollution from petroleum and petrochemical facilities across the country , including in Sarnia , Mississauga , Montr ? al , Burnaby , Prince George , Saint John , and many communities in Alberta and Saskatchewan . <p> Harmful airborne substances -- known as volatile organic compounds -- emitted from these facilities contribute to premature deaths and more frequent and severe asthma symptoms , and they force workers and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Government of Canada worked closely with industry to provide many compliance options to minimize costs . As a result , industries can find the most effective ways to reduce their pollution . Many of the new requirements to reduce air pollution are already in place for similar facilities in the US . These measures support competitiveness as the petroleum and petrochemical sectors begin to recover from the economic downturn and low energy prices . <p> Through these measures , the Government of Canada is working to protect human health and the environment and strengthening the clean economy . <p> The regulations also support clean growth in Canada 's energy sector and complement the commitment to meet and exceed the country 's 2030 emissions-reduction target and achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 . <p> Copies of the final regulations will be published in the Canada Gazette , Part II , on November 11 . <p> Quotes <p> " The pandemic has reminded us how important access to nature and fresh air is to our everyday life and well-being . Our government is proud to be working directly with cities , Indigenous communities @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ our air quality . These new regulations will contribute to the health of Canadians while ensuring the prosperity of our economy and protecting jobs today . " -- The Honourable Jonathan Wilkinson , Minister of Environment and Climate Change <p> " I have always been supportive of improving the air quality and environment for our community while preserving our economic competitiveness and prosperity . " -- Mike Bradley , Mayor of the City of Sarnia <p> Quick facts <p> The regulations will lead to $192 million in health benefits from 2021 to 2037 . Health benefits include an estimated 34 fewer premature deaths ; almost 6,900 fewer days without asthma symptoms ; and over 33,600 fewer days of restricted activity . <p> By inspecting and repairing leaks , the oil and gas industry will avoid losing valuable fuel products , which are also released with **25;373;TOOLONG emissions . Stopping the leaks will generate revenue of around $49 million for the oil and gas industry , between 2021 and 2037 . <p> Canada 's carbon-pollution pricing system and the Clean Fuel Standard ( in development ) include emissions-credit-trading systems that will @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and gas facilities . These systems work by creating incentives for refineries , upgraders , and petrochemical facilities to become more efficient and reduce pollution . <p> Through a partnership between the Government of Canada , the Aamjiwnaang First Nation , and the Province of Ontario , a permanent air-quality monitoring station provides continuous and real-time data for the Aamjiwnaang First Nation community that borders Sarnia 's refinery and petrochemical district . Data collected will be useful to inform next steps in addressing local air-quality issues . 
@@52189156 <p> General view of the Pickering Nuclear Power Generating Station , April 17 , 2019 . <p> CARLOS OSORIO/Reuters <p> John Gorman is the president and CEO of the Canadian Nuclear Association . <p> Undisputedly , nuclear must be in the energy mix for Canada to reach its greenhouse gas emissions reductions targets . Minister of Natural Resources Seamus O'Regan recently said as much when he stated that the federal government has " not seen a credible model where we can get to net-zero emissions by 2050 without nuclear . " <p> It 's about time . Nuclear power is a clean energy . It does not emit carbon or pollutants that harm human health and the environment , and it 's the only energy source that delivers carbon-free , reliable heat and electricity around the clock . As a result , new nuclear -- specifically , small modular reactors ( SMRs ) -- are uniquely positioned to decarbonize our extraction industries , provide heat and power to First Nations communities , and work in tandem with innovations in renewables . <p> Story continues below advertisement <p> Of course , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in nuclear represents " putting all of our eggs in one basket . " We hear that nuclear technology is too far off in the distance to be useful now . We hear that there are worries about how we can manage the byproducts safely . But these concerns are not always rooted in facts , science or reality . <p> To begin , renewable energy sources can and do work in partnership with nuclear . The issue of climate change is so colossal that we must leverage a multitude of tools in our box to work together . This includes finding the right complementary energy mix for Canadians , and the right balance in terms of regulation and policy . Around 16 to 19 per cent of our energy comes from renewables . There is plenty of room to grow , but we can not rely solely on renewables down the road -- and I say that as the former president and CEO of Canadian Solar Industries . We must also bear in mind that around 80 per cent of energy demand today is met by fossil fuels and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ met by renewables alone , without nuclear . <p> Fighting climate change is a journey , albeit one we must accelerate . But new nuclear technology is around the corner , with initiatives in Russia , China , Argentina , Sweden and the U.S. attracting investment and approaching completion . Here in Canada , 12 projects are going through review and approval . We are on the brink of activating the next generation of new nuclear through SMRs with a projected nine-year roadmap . That may seem like a long timeline , but for context , Canada 's plan to phase out coal takes place over 31 years . Our emissions goals targets for 2030 and 2050 will not happen through quick fixes . Delaying efforts on next-generation nuclear technology because it would take too long is a nonsensical argument : We need to act now to productively advance these capabilities . Global investments in wind and solar over these last two decades is what enabled us to benefit from that clean technology today . <p> We also sometimes hear detractors making a case that we should n't focus on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ innovation requires investment ; that 's the nature of social-economic progress , and has been for centuries . At the same time , the government has pointed to the potential economic contribution of SMRs , with a conservatively estimated domestic value of $5.3-billion between 2025 and 2040 ( $150-billion globally per annum ) . It 's an industry that not only solves an enormously expensive problem -- the consequences of the climate crisis could wreak potentially massive costs -- but would also drive economic prosperity for Canada . <p> Finally , there 's the issue of waste -- a result of all energy sources , even wind and solar farms , given their finite life cycles . Nuclear , however , is the only energy industry that accounts for all its byproducts . While some industries send waste into the air , the nuclear industry 's by-products are safely stored or recycled , managed and monitored in a highly regulated environment . Canada is recognized as a world leader in nuclear fuel management ; scientists and experts visit to learn from our processes , which are built on 65 years @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the public has ever been harmed by the storage or transportation of radioactive by-products . Looking to the future , nuclear -- unlike any other sources of energy -- also presents the opportunity to recycle its waste products . This means it may be possible that waste currently being held in repositories could be converted into fuel in the future . <p> Climate change is a complicated issue that requires a holistic and balanced approach . It will demand a united effort to move down the path of a cleaner oil and gas industry . And that collective journey on the part of Canadians should be undergirded by facts and science . <p> Keep your Opinions sharp and informed . Get the Opinion newsletter . @@52189774 <p> Hydrogen can play a key role in decarbonising rail travel too , alongside other low-carbon fuels , such as biofuels . ( Pexels Photo ) <p> Is hydrogen the lifeblood of a low-carbon future , or an overhyped distraction from real solutions ? One thing is certain -- the coal , oil and natural gas which currently power much of daily life must be phased out within coming decades . From the cars we drive to the energy that heats our homes , these fossil fuels are deeply embedded in society and the global economy . But is the best solution in all cases to swap them with hydrogen -- a fuel which only produces water vapour , and not CO2 , when burned ? <p> Answering that question are six experts in engineering , physics and chemistry . <h> Road and rail <p> Hu Li , Associate Professor of Energy Engineering , University of Leeds <p> Transport became the UK 's largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in 2016 , contributing about 28% of the country 's total . <p> Replacing the internal combustion engines of passenger cars @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ decarbonising road transport , but electrification is n't such a good option for heavy-duty vehicles such as lorries and buses . Compared to gasoline and diesel fuels , the energy density ( measured in megajoules per kilogram ) of a battery is just 1% . For a 40-tonne truck , just over four tonnes of lithium-ion battery cells are needed for a range of 800 kilometres , compared to just 220 kilograms of diesel . <p> With the UK government set to ban fossil fuel vehicles from 2035 , hydrogen fuel cells could do much of the heavy lifting in decarbonising freight and public transport , where 80% of hydrogen demand in transport is likely to come from . <p> A fuel cell generates electricity through a chemical reaction between the stored hydrogen and oxygen , producing water and hot air as a byproduct . Vehicles powered by hydrogen fuel cells have a similar driving range and can be refuelled about as quickly as internal combustion engine vehicles , another reason they 're useful for long-haul and heavy-duty transport . <p> Hydrogen fuel can be transported as liquid or compressed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ millions on infrastructure and speed up its deployment . Even existing internal combustion engines can use hydrogen , but there are problems with fuel injection , reduced power output , onboard storage and emissions of nitrogen oxides ( NO ? ) , which can react in the lower atmosphere to form ozone -- a greenhouse gas . The goal should be to eventually replace internal combustion engines with hydrogen fuel cells in vehicles that are too large for lithium-ion batteries . But in the meantime , blending with other fuels or using a diesel-hydrogen hybrid could help lower emissions . <p> It 's very important to consider where the hydrogen comes from though . Hydrogen can be produced by splitting water with electricity in a process called electrolysis . If the electricity was generated by renewable sources such as solar and wind , the resulting fuel is called green hydrogen . It can be used in the form of compressed gas or liquid and converted to methane , methanol , ammonia and other synthetic liquid fuels . <p> But nearly all of the 27 terawatt-hours ( TWh ) of hydrogen @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fuels , which generates nine tonnes of CO2 for every tonne of hydrogen . This is currently the cheapest option , though some experts predict that green hydrogen will be cost-competitive by 2030 . In the meantime , governments will need to ramp up the production of vehicles with hydrogen fuel cells and storage tanks and build lots of refuelling points . <p> Hydrogen can play a key role in decarbonising rail travel too , alongside other low-carbon fuels , such as biofuels . In the UK , 6,049 kilometres of mainline routes run on electricity -- that 's 38% of the total . Trains powered by hydrogen fuel cells offer a zero-emission alternative to diesel trains . <p> The Coradia iLint , which entered commercial service in Germany in 2018 , is the world 's first hydrogen-powered train . The UK recently launched mainline testing of its own hydrogen-powered train , though the UK trial aims to retrofit existing diesel trains rather than design and build entirely new ones . <h> Aviation <p> Valeska Ting , Professor of Smart Nanomaterials , University of Bristol <p> Of all of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ perhaps the most challenging . While cars and boats can realistically switch to batteries or hybrid technologies , the sheer weight of even the lightest batteries makes long-haul electric air travel tricky . <p> Single-seat concept planes such as the Solar Impulse generate their energy from the sun , but they ca n't generate enough based on the efficiency of current solar cells alone so must also use batteries . Other alternatives include synthetic fuels or biofuels , but these could just defer or reduce carbon emissions , rather than eliminate them altogether , as a carbon-free fuel like green hydrogen could . <p> Hydrogen is extremely light and contains three times more energy per kilogram than jet fuel , which is why it 's traditionally used to power rockets . Companies including Airbus are already developing commercial zero-emission aircraft that run on hydrogen . This involves a radical redesign of their fleet to accommodate liquid hydrogen fuel tanks . <p> There are some technical challenges though . Hydrogen is a gas at room temperature , so very low temperatures and special equipment are needed to store it as a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ more fuel . However , research we 're doing at the Bristol Composites Institute is helping with the design of lightweight aircraft components made out of composite materials . We 're also looking at nanoporous materials that behave like molecular sponges , spontaneously absorbing and storing hydrogen at high densities for onboard hydrogen storage in future aircraft designs . <p> France and Germany are investing billions in hydrogen-powered passenger aircraft . But while the development of these new aircraft by industry continues apace , international airports will also need to rapidly invest in infrastructure to store and deliver liquid hydrogen to refuel them . There 's a risk that fleets of hydrogen aeroplanes could take off before there 's a sufficient fuel supply chain to sustain them . <h> Heating <p> If the All Party Parliamentary Group on Hydrogen 's recommendations are taken up , the UK government is likely to support hydrogen as a replacement fuel for heating buildings in its next white paper . The other option for decarbonising Britain 's gas heating network is electricity . So which is likely to be a better choice -- a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ? <p> First there 's the price of fuel to consider . When hydrogen is generated through electrolysis , between 30-40% of the original electric energy is lost . One kilowatt-hour ( kWh ) of electricity in a heat pump may generate 3-5 kWh of heat , while the same kWh of electricity gets you only 0.6-0.7 kWh of heat with a hydrogen-fuelled boiler . This means that generating enough hydrogen fuel to heat a home will require electricity generated from four times as many turbines and solar panels than a heat pump . Because heat pumps need so much less energy overall to supply the same amount of heat , the need for large amounts of stored green energy on standby is much less . Even reducing these losses with more advanced technology , hydrogen will remain relatively expensive , both in terms of energy and money . <p> So using hydrogen to heat homes is n't cheap for consumers . Granted , there is a higher upfront cost for installing an electric heat pump . That could be a serious drawback for cash-strapped households , though heat pumps @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of hydrogen . In time , lower fuel bills would more than cover the installation cost . <p> Replacing natural gas with hydrogen in the UK 's heating network is n't likely to be simple either . Per volume , the energy density of hydrogen gas is about one-third that of natural gas , so converting to hydrogen will not only require new boilers , but also investment in grids to increase how much fuel they can deliver . The very small size of hydrogen molecules mean they 're much more prone to leaking than natural gas molecules . Ensuring that the existing gas distribution system is fit for hydrogen could prove quite costly . <p> In high-density housing in inner cities , district heating systems -- which distribute waste heat from power plants and factories into homes -- could be a better bet in a warming climate , as , like heat pumps , they can cool homes as well as heat them . <p> Above all , this stresses the importance of energy efficiency , what the International Energy Agency calls the first fuel in buildings . @@52190086 <h> The Future of Health and Well-being <p> At some point in our lives we all struggle not just with our mental health but also our physical health . After all , biologically speaking we humans were only designed to live to around the age of 30 , and societally speaking our minds were never designed to withstand the mental onslaught that we experience now -- whether from today 's lifestyles or the often-overwhelming impact of being plugged into and aware of almost every event on the planet , no matter how big or small . <p> With more than 8 billion people living on our pale blue dot , a population growing at an average rate of just over 1 percent per year , and expected to top 10 billion by 2050 , it 's clear that in the future there 's going to be an even greater demand for health and wellness services of all kinds -- that is , if we 're all going to live long and happy lives . <p> Today various independent organisations estimate that about 13 percent of the world 's population , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of mental disorder , and that on a yearly basis a further 800 million are affected by cardiovascular disease , cancers , neurological , neonatal , and respiratory disorders -- all before we dig into the number of people who are affected by serious injury , which records suggest is at least another 250 million , with other diseases adding a further 400 million into the mix . <p> The back-of-a-Post-It calculation therefore means that at any particular point in time almost 2.5 billion people on our planet " are n't feeling well . " And that 's all before we think about the future impact that climate change , environmental destruction , pollution , poor diet , stress , and other factors will have on our long-term health and well-being . <p> When you dig into the data further , another surprising fact is that in spite of an increasingly aging global population , only 35 percent of people over age 50 suffer from some form of affliction versus 65 percent below the age of 50 . Only the under-under 5 age group has seen steady and continuous reduction @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with the Old Diseases , in with the New <p> Since 1990 , though , when countries started keeping more comprehensive health records , the kinds of afflictions we suffer from have changed significantly . There 's been an enormous decrease in the number of people suffering from diarrhea and common infectious diseases as well as from neonatal disorders and nutritional deficiencies . On the other hand , there 's been a marked increase in the number of people afflicted by so-called " modern age " diseases including cancer , cardiovascular and respiratory diseases -- as well as , perhaps unsurprisingly given the pressures of modern life , mental disorders . <p> Old Age Becomes the Norm <p> As for the big one , though -- life expectancy -- except for what hopefully turns out to be nothing more than a blip in recent U.S. data , in which life expectancy recently fell for the first time since 1918 -- overall global life expectancy has surged from an estimated 32 years in the year 1900 , when most records began , to an average of 72 today , with countries @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the global charts with average life expectancies between 81 and 83 . <p> As we look to the future , and certainly here in the West , more biotech and healthcare organisations are talking in terms of " defeating death " rather than just " conquering disease . " Many believe they can reach what they term " escape velocity , " the point at which advances in healthcare will add more than a year 's worth of life to people for every year that passes , by the year 2028 . And if recent sci-fi like breakthroughs are anything to go by , they could be onto something . <p> Now , with the bases covered , let 's have a deeper look at what the future of healthcare , which is by far and away one of the most active sectors I track , has in store for us all . <p> A Revolution for Mental Health <p> It 's no surprise that the pressures of everyday life and an always-on society -- in which people are continuously bombarded by all manner of events that are often then @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fractured and fractious leadership , and trolls , among many other things , including the recent pandemic -- are taking their toll on mental health . <p> Further , the rate of change is accelerating and every cultural corner , industry , and segment of society is being disrupted and transformed at an unimaginable rate in previously unimaginable ways , presenting the omnipresent spectre of global displacement and job automation . You could easily argue that the mental pressure people experience is only going to increase and that a toxic cocktail is brewing , one that , left unchecked , could turn into the mental equivalent of a Molotov cocktail , with consequences for individuals and society at large . <p> When it comes to tackling what experts around the world are increasingly calling a mental health crisis , there are a number of tall obstacles that need to be overcome . First , there 's the issue of identifying sufferers . Second , there 's the issue of correctly diagnosing symptoms and their root causes . Finally there 's the no-small-matter of providing the right-point-in-time support and appropriate follow-up @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are struggling has always fallen on their shoulders or those of the people around them -- colleagues , family , and friends , who , societally at least , have hitherto been expected to be able to identify the symptoms and surface the issues so they can start getting the help and support they need . Of course , few , if any , of the people involved in this first and arguably most crucial step are n't trained professionals , which often means that sufferers ' problems either go unnoticed or undiagnosed . So sufferers never receive the support they need , which can sometimes have tragic consequences . <p> Once an issue has been identified , being able to accurately diagnose it and its cause in order to prescribe the right treatment is also difficult , even for professionals . Then there 's the issue of what happens and how those struggling fare when they 're out of arm 's length of the people who are there to support them . <p> When the issues are looked at holistically , it 's clear to see the gaps that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ trained professionals , and other areas -- and that far too many people fall between the cracks , some never to re-emerge . Fortunately , technology provides a number of new tools and solutions we can leverage . The majority are digital , powered by AI , and can be easily accessed by billions of connected people via computers , tablets , smart assistants , smart devices , and even connected home devices . <p> Take the humble smartphone , a rich source of information if ever there was one . Today , an accurate measure of your mental health can be gleaned by analysing the way you use your phone , the angles at which you hold it at , how often and how fast you pick it up , what you type and how fast you type it , the speed at which you scroll -- and that 's before discussing how it can be used to monitor your posture , analyse your voice patterns , and track your minute-by-minute movements , or how the camera can gather a whole host of interesting biometric data . <p> Many @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ everything from the onset of dementia and PTSD all the way to depression and even a person 's inclination to suicide -- better than even the best human experts . <p> From a support perspective , some of the same AI-powered platforms are using many of the same privacy-busting techniques -- an issue for another post -- to provide point-in-time Robo-counselling services that cost little to nothing and that are always with you , no matter where you are .
